prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and the development of incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B023 first, but unanimity is not itself evidence; the case rests on the science. GLP-1 work runs from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect to long-acting agonists, a chain in which each step was a genuine discovery. It has changed care for type 2 diabetes and obesity and has outcome-trial support for cardiovascular and renal benefit, from many independent groups over more than a decade. The mechanism is settled, the clinical effect is large, and the recognition is timely. A single-achievement prize also avoids splitting credit across unrelated fields. Holst and Drucker supply the physiology and biology, and Knudsen supplies the engineering of long-acting acylated analogues, without which the biology would not have become a drug.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. The credited list has four names and a prize has at most three. Mojsov's identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is a real claim, and Habener, who is not on the list, has a related one. Any three-person choice leaves out someone with a defensible claim. The prize could also be read as a compound of academic physiology and industrial optimisation, which is a fair objection to including Knudsen. B051 (unfolded protein response) has cleaner two-person credit and a purer discovery narrative, though a smaller medical footprint.

responses.point: Linnarsson would credit Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, treating Knudsen's work as industrial optimisation and Mojsov as the identifier of the active peptide form.
responses.response: This is the most substantive disagreement with my opening and I take it seriously. I still keep Knudsen over Mojsov. Without long-acting analogues, GLP-1 biology remains a physiological observation, because the native peptide has a half-life of minutes. Designing acylated, albumin-binding analogues and taking them through to semaglutide was a scientific step, not only a manufacturing one. The Mojsov claim is real but contested, and I cannot settle priority from the supplied evidence. If the committee judges that the prize is about the basic discovery, I would accept Mojsov in the third place, and I would then want the citation worded narrowly enough not to imply that the drug development is credited.

responses.point: Perlmann sees Mojsov's credit as credible but contested, finds Knudsen's industrial development a less natural fit for a three-person prize, and notes that Habener and Bell are not on the list, so any configuration is incomplete.
responses.response: I agree on incompleteness and on the priority dispute, which is why I frame B023 as the incretin-physiology-to-therapy chain rather than the identification of a single peptide. I disagree that industrial origin should disqualify Knudsen; therapeutic development can be recognised when it rests on and extends the underlying biology. The open question is whether the committee can state a rationale for Mojsov that does not depend on resolving the Habener priority question. If it cannot, leaving that name out is the more defensible position.

responses.point: Svenningsson, as chair, supports B023 with Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, notes that Mojsov's and Habener's contributions are contested, and ranks the unfolded protein response (B051) second as a clean, fundamental pathway discovery.
responses.response: I agree on B023 and on the configuration. On B051 I agree that the Mori and Walter attribution is cleaner than anything else on the shortlist. Where I differ slightly is on the weight of the translational gap: I would see B051 as an excellent next-in-line prize rather than a competitor for this year. I keep it as an alternative, since if the committee cannot agree on GLP-1 attribution, B051 is the candidate that can be agreed on most quickly and with the least dispute over names.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius includes Mojsov alongside Drucker and Holst, says the question is whether basic discovery or drug development is the core, and ranks Krainer and Bennett's SMN2 antisense work (B050) fourth.
responses.response: I agree that the basic-versus-development question decides the third name. On B050 I see mechanistic clarity and major patient benefit, but I rank it lower because the advance can be read as engineering an established modality, and because the SMN gene discovery that made it possible lies outside the credited names. It is a strong future candidate rather than one I would put in the preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the third laureate should be Knudsen or Mojsov depends on whether the committee treats the core achievement as basic discovery or as discovery plus drug development, and I cannot resolve the Mojsov and Habener priority question from the supplied record.
Whether leaving out Habener, who is not in the credited list, distorts the historical account of the prize.
Whether the compound basic-and-industrial character of B023 is an acceptable single achievement.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My Karolinska Institutet affiliation and past co-authorship with colleagues such as Linnarsson and Frisen concern single-cell and neurogenesis work, which is not on this shortlist, and I do not infer any personal tie to the B023 candidates.
